  - title: 'Ammo Goes Boom: December 7, 1941 Wasn’t the Only Pearl Harbor Disaster the
      Navy Suffered'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/ammo-goes-boom-december-7-1941-wasnt-the-only-pearl-harbor-disaster-the-navy-suffered/
    text: 'Key Points and Summary – Pearl Harbor has a second, forgotten catastrophe.
      On May 21, 1944, West Loch—packed with LSTs loaded for the Saipan invasion—erupted
      in a chain of explosions and fires. -Fuel ignited on the water, burning debris
      rained over a wide radius, and blasts continued for hours as ships tried to get
      underway. […] The post Ammo Goes Boom: December 7, 1941 Wasn’t the Only Pearl
      Harbor Disaster the Navy Suffered appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: On May 21, 1944, a lesser-known disaster at West Loch in Pearl
      Harbor involved a catastrophic series of explosions and fires from LSTs preparing
      for the Saipan invasion, resulting in widespread destruction and chaos.
    paragraph_summary: On May 21, 1944, a significant but often overlooked disaster
      occurred at West Loch, Pearl Harbor, when a series of explosions and fires erupted
      from LSTs (Landing Ship Tanks) loaded for the Saipan invasion. The incident involved
      ignited fuel on the water, resulting in burning debris scattered over a wide area,
      and the explosions persisted for hours as ships attempted to escape. This event
      highlights that the Navy faced another catastrophic incident at Pearl Harbor beyond
      the well-known attack on December 7, 1941.

    text: 'Key Points and Summary – The 1985 K-431 Russian Navy nuclear submarine accident

      a catastrophic refueling incident that resulted in a reactor explosion, scattering
      radioactive debris and leaving nearby responders and towns uninformed due to Soviet
      secrecy.
    paragraph_summary: The 1985 K-431 accident involving a Russian Navy nuclear submarine
      was a catastrophic refueling incident at Chazhma Bay, near Vladivostok, rather
      than a battle loss. During the handling of the reactor lid, an over-lift caused
      a prompt criticality, resulting in an explosion that destroyed the reactor and
      dispersed radioactive debris across nearby ships, docks, and the shoreline. The
      Soviet government's secrecy surrounding the incident left both responders and
      local communities largely uninformed about the dangers and consequences of the
      explosion.

      secrecy.

      than a battle loss. During the handling of the reactor lid, an over-lift caused
      a prompt criticality, resulting in an explosion that destroyed the reactor and
      dispersed radioactive debris across nearby ships, docks, and the shoreline. The

      to ensure air superiority through advanced technology and integrated systems.

      environments. This innovative approach could effectively merge the functionalities
      of aircraft carriers and submarines.

    text: Key Points and Summary – USS Nimitz (CVN-68), commissioned in 1975, is the

      capacity make early retirement sensible. -Supporters counter that Ford-class delays—especially

    paragraph_summary: The USS Nimitz (CVN-68), commissioned in 1975, is the oldest
      active aircraft carrier in the world and represents U.S. naval strength. While
      some critics advocate for its early retirement due to its age, the expensive Refueling
      and Complex Overhaul process, and limited shipyard capacity, supporters argue
      against this move, citing delays in the Ford-class carriers, particularly the
      late arrival of the USS John F. Kennedy. This ongoing debate highlights the challenges
      the U.S. Navy faces in balancing the operational needs of aging vessels with the
      development of new ones.

    paragraph_summary: The debate over retiring the A-10 Warthog revolves around its
      survivability and relevance in modern warfare, as it is slow, non-stealthy, and

      close air support (CAS) roles, allowing for a reallocation of funding towards
      more advanced military priorities. However, there are significant counterarguments
      regarding the A-10's unique capabilities and its effectiveness in specific combat
      scenarios, suggesting that the decision to retire the aircraft is not straightforward.

    text: 'Key Points and Summary – The Joint Strike Fighter competition (1997–2001)
      pitted Lockheed Martin’s X-35 against Boeing’s X-32 to create a multi-role stealth
      aircraft with three variants: conventional, STOVL, and carrier. -The X-35 gained
      an edge by demonstrating more efficient STOVL operations without major airframe
      changes, reassuring evaluators with a design closer to its original […] The post
      Forget the F-22, F-35 or F-47 NGAD: X-32 Stealth Fighter Has a Message for the
      Air Force appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The Joint Strike Fighter competition (1997–2001) saw Lockheed
      Martin's X-35 outperform Boeing's X-32 by showcasing superior STOVL capabilities
      and a design that remained true to its original concept, ultimately leading to
      the development of a versatile multi-role stealth aircraft.
    paragraph_summary: 'The Joint Strike Fighter competition from 1997 to 2001 featured
      Lockheed Martin''s X-35 and Boeing''s X-32, aiming to develop a versatile stealth
      aircraft with three variants: conventional, short takeoff and vertical landing
      (STOVL), and carrier-based. The X-35 ultimately prevailed by showcasing superior
      STOVL capabilities without significant modifications to its airframe, which instilled
      confidence in evaluators regarding its design fidelity. The article suggests that
      despite the advancements of the F-22, F-35, and the upcoming F-47 Next Generation
      Air Dominance (NGAD), the X-32 still holds relevant lessons for the Air Force.'

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/military-quote-of-the-day-by-general-george-patton-better-to-fight-for-something-than-live-for-nothing/
    text: 'Key Points and Summary – George S. Patton Jr. remains one of America’s most
      quotable and polarizing commanders—battlefield genius and hard-driving disciplinarian.
      -Born in 1885, he battled dyslexia, yet pushed through VMI and West Point, competed
      in the 1912 Olympics, and saw action on the Pancho Villa Expedition. -In World
      War I he helped pioneer […] The post Military Quote of the Day by General George
      Patton: ‘Better to fight for something than live for nothing’ appeared first on
      19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: General George S. Patton Jr., a renowned and controversial
      military leader known for his battlefield brilliance and strict discipline, overcame
      personal challenges to achieve significant military accomplishments, including
      pioneering tank warfare in World War I and competing in the 1912 Olympics.
    paragraph_summary: General George S. Patton Jr., born in 1885, is remembered as
      a highly quotable and controversial military leader known for his battlefield
      brilliance and strict discipline. Despite facing challenges like dyslexia, he
      successfully graduated from Virginia Military Institute and West Point, competed
      in the 1912 Olympics, and participated in the Pancho Villa Expedition. His contributions
      during World War I helped to pioneer modern armored warfare, and he is famously
      quoted as saying, "Better to fight for something than live for nothing," reflecting
      his belief in the importance of purpose and valor in military service.

  - title: A U.S. Navy Nuclear Powered Submarine Sank 220 Miles East of Cape Cod, Massachusetts
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/a-u-s-navy-nuclear-powered-submarine-sank-220-miles-east-of-cape-cod-massachusetts/
    text: Key Points and Summary – USS Thresher’s sinking on April 10, 1963—during deep-dive
      trials off Cape Cod—remains a defining cautionary tale for the U.S. Navy as it
      fields modern Columbia- and Virginia-class submarines. After garbled communications
      with the support ship Skylark, Thresher was lost with 129 aboard and later found
      shattered on the seafloor. -Investigators […] The post A U.S. Navy Nuclear Powered
      Submarine Sank 220 Miles East of Cape Cod, Massachusetts appeared first on 19FortyFive
      .
    one_sentence_summary: The sinking of the USS Thresher during deep-dive trials in
      1963, which resulted in the loss of 129 crew members, serves as a critical warning
      for the U.S. Navy as it continues to develop modern submarines.
    paragraph_summary: The sinking of the USS Thresher on April 10, 1963, during deep-dive
      trials off Cape Cod serves as a critical warning for the U.S. Navy as it continues
      to deploy modern Columbia- and Virginia-class submarines. Following unclear communications
      with the support ship Skylark, the Thresher was lost with all 129 crew members
      aboard and was later discovered shattered on the ocean floor. This incident has
      had a lasting impact on submarine safety protocols and operational procedures
      within the Navy.
    published: '2025-12-20T12:37:45+00:00'

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/u-s-navy-problem-is-the-era-of-surface-warships-coming-to-an-end/
    text: 'Key Points and Summary – Drone swarms, cruise missiles, and cheap loitering
      munitions have made modern surface warships look like easy prey. -But that verdict
      freezes the story at the “action” phase of war. Precision strike is proliferating,
      sensors are everywhere, and kill chains are faster—especially in the littorals.
      -The “reaction” is already underway: layered […] The post U.S. Navy Problem: Is
      the Era of Surface Warships Coming to An End? appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The article discusses how advancements in drone technology,
      cruise missiles, and loitering munitions have made modern surface warships vulnerable,
      prompting a shift towards layered defense strategies in response to evolving warfare
      dynamics.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the vulnerability of modern surface warships
      in the face of advanced military technologies such as drone swarms, cruise missiles,
      and inexpensive loitering munitions, which have led to perceptions of these vessels
      as easy targets. However, it argues that this assessment overlooks the evolving
      nature of warfare, particularly the "reaction" phase, where militaries are adapting
      to these threats through layered defense systems and enhanced capabilities. As
      precision strikes and rapid kill chains become more prevalent, especially in coastal
      areas, the U.S. Navy is exploring ways to ensure the continued relevance and effectiveness
      of surface warships in modern combat scenarios.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/antigua-and-barbuda-dominica-hit-by-new-u-s-entry-limits/
    text: Key Points and Summary – President Trump’s December 16 proclamation expands
      U.S. travel restrictions, adding partial limits on Antigua and Barbuda and Dominica
      effective January 1. -The White House cites “citizenship-by-investment” programs
      that historically issued passports without a residency requirement. -Tourism operators
      and insurers warn fewer travelers could mean emptier flights, weaker hotel demand,
      and […] The post Antigua and Barbuda, Dominica Hit by New U.S. Entry Limits appeared
      first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: President Trump's December 16 proclamation expands U.S. travel
      restrictions to include partial limits on Antigua and Barbuda and Dominica, effective
      January 1, due to concerns over their citizenship-by-investment programs, which
      may negatively impact tourism and travel demand.
    paragraph_summary: On December 16, President Trump announced an expansion of U.S.
      travel restrictions, which will impose partial entry limits on Antigua and Barbuda
      and Dominica starting January 1. The White House's rationale for these restrictions
      is linked to the countries' "citizenship-by-investment" programs that have allowed
      the issuance of passports without requiring residency. This move has raised concerns
      among tourism operators and insurers, who warn that a decrease in travelers could
      lead to reduced flight occupancy and weakened demand for hotels in these nations.

  - title: Mach 3 SR-71 Blackbird Was So Advanced It Needed ‘Custom Fuel’ to Fly
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/mach-3-sr-71-blackbird-was-so-advanced-it-needed-custom-fuel-to-fly/
    text: 'Key Points and Summary – The SR-71 Blackbird’s extreme speed and heat demands
      drove the creation of a dedicated fuel: JP-7. Conventional jet fuels were too
      volatile for the temperatures generated at sustained Mach 3 flight, creating unacceptable
      fire risk. -JP-7 solved the safety problem by being highly stable and difficult
      to ignite—but that introduced […] The post Mach 3 SR-71 Blackbird Was So Advanced
      It Needed ‘Custom Fuel’ to Fly appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The SR-71 Blackbird required a specialized fuel, JP-7, due
      to its extreme speed and heat at Mach 3, as conventional jet fuels posed a fire
      risk at those temperatures.
    paragraph_summary: The SR-71 Blackbird, known for its remarkable speed capabilities
      at Mach 3, required a specialized fuel, JP-7, due to the extreme temperatures
      generated during flight that conventional jet fuels could not withstand. Standard
      fuels posed a significant fire risk due to their volatility at such high speeds,
      while JP-7 was designed to be highly stable and resistant to ignition, addressing
      safety concerns. However, this stability also presented challenges in terms of
      ignition and performance, highlighting the advanced engineering required for the
      Blackbird's operation.
    published: '2025-12-19T19:53:47+00:00'

  - title: Why Doesn’t the US Military Have Stealth Helicopters?
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/why-doesnt-the-us-military-have-stealth-helicopters/
    text: Key Points and Summary – The U.S. doesn’t field “true stealth” helicopters
      at scale because rotary-wing physics fights stealth at every turn. -Spinning rotor
      blades and complex hubs reflect radar, engines and exhaust produce strong infrared
      signatures, and helicopter acoustics can give away position long before radar
      matters. -Helicopters also fly low and slow, often […] The post Why Doesn’t the
      US Military Have Stealth Helicopters? appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: The U.S. military lacks "true stealth" helicopters due to
      the inherent challenges of rotary-wing design, which makes them susceptible to
      radar, infrared detection, and acoustic signatures.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the challenges the U.S. military faces
      in developing "true stealth" helicopters, highlighting that the physics of rotary-wing
      aircraft inherently conflicts with stealth capabilities. Factors such as spinning
      rotor blades and complex hub designs create radar reflections, while engines and
      exhaust emit significant infrared signatures. Additionally, helicopters' low and
      slow flight patterns make them vulnerable to detection through sound long before
      radar becomes a factor. Consequently, these limitations hinder the effective deployment
      of stealth helicopters at scale.
    published: '2025-12-19T17:33:10+00:00'

  - title: 'Forget the MiG-41, PAK DA or Su-47: Russia’s BMPT “Terminator” Tank Is a

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/forget-the-mig-41-pak-da-or-su-47-russias-bmpt-terminator-tank-is-a-frankenstein-failure/
    text: 'Key Points and Summary – Russia’s BMPT “Terminator” was conceived as a tank-based
      escort vehicle that could protect armored columns in cities, forests, and mountains.
      -The idea dates to Soviet-era experiments, but post-Chechnya redesigns stripped
      out dismount infantry and produced a heavily armed, five-man platform with twin
      30mm cannons, Ataka missiles, and grenade launchers on […] The post Forget the
      MiG-41, PAK DA or Su-47: Russia’s BMPT “Terminator” Tank Is a Frankenstein Failure
      appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: Russia's BMPT "Terminator," originally designed as a tank-based
      escort vehicle to protect armored units in various terrains, has been criticized
      as a flawed and ineffective military platform due to its heavy armament and lack
      of infantry support.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses Russia's BMPT "Terminator," a tank-based
      escort vehicle designed to protect armored columns in various terrains, a concept
      rooted in Soviet-era experiments. Following redesigns after the Chechen War, the
      vehicle evolved into a heavily armed platform featuring twin 30mm cannons, Ataka
      missiles, and grenade launchers, but ultimately, it has been labeled a "Frankenstein
      failure." The piece argues that despite its advanced weaponry, the BMPT has not
      met expectations and is overshadowed by other military projects like the MiG-41
      and PAK DA.

    one_sentence_summary: The Montana-class super-battleship, designed to be more formidable
      than the Iowa class with twelve 16-inch guns and heavy armor, would have been
      less impactful in World War II had it been completed in 1944-45, primarily serving
      in support roles rather than engaging in direct naval combat.
    paragraph_summary: The Montana-class was a proposed super-battleship for the U.S.
      Navy, designed to be larger, more powerful, and better armored than the Iowa class,
      featuring twelve 16-inch guns and armor comparable to Japan's Yamato. However,
      the timing of its development was critical; had the Montana-class ships been completed
      and deployed in 1944-45, they would likely have been utilized primarily for shore
      bombardment and fleet screening rather than engaging in direct naval battles.
      The article suggests that the lessons from the Montana-class's design and intended
      role hold relevance for the current U.S. Navy.

  - title: 'Forget the F-22 or F-35: China’s Stealth Fighters Might Soon Be Invisible
      to Space-Based Radar'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/forger-the-f-22-or-f-35-chinas-stealth-fighters-might-soon-be-invisible-to-space-based-radar/
    text: 'Key Points and Summary – Chinese researchers linked to CASIC report a microwave-absorbing
      aircraft coating for stealth fighters and bombers that is derived from dried loofah
      and aims to reduce detection by space-based radar. -The process carbonizes loofah
      into a porous carbon network and embeds nickel-cobalt oxide (NiCo₂O₄) nanoparticles,
      producing an NCO-2 composite layer about […] The post Forget the F-22 or F-35:
      China’s Stealth Fighters Might Soon Be Invisible to Space-Based Radar appeared
      first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: Chinese researchers have developed a microwave-absorbing aircraft
      coating made from carbonized loofah and embedded nickel-cobalt oxide nanoparticles,
      which aims to enhance the stealth capabilities of fighters and bombers against
      space-based radar detection.
    paragraph_summary: Chinese researchers from the China Aerospace Science and Industry
      Corporation (CASIC) have developed a microwave-absorbing coating for stealth aircraft,
      including fighters and bombers, derived from dried loofah. This innovative coating
      aims to enhance stealth capabilities by reducing detection by space-based radar.
      The process involves carbonizing loofah to create a porous carbon network, which
      is then infused with nickel-cobalt oxide (NiCo₂O₄) nanoparticles, resulting in
      a composite layer known as NCO-2. This advancement could potentially make China's
      stealth fighters less detectable compared to existing models like the F-22 and
      F-35.
    published: '2025-12-18T12:28:45+00:00'

  - title: U.S. Army and U.S. Navy Miscalculated Number of Low-Scoring Recruits Entering
      U.S. Military, IG Finds
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/u-s-army-and-u-s-navy-miscalculated-number-of-low-scoring-recruits-entering-u-s-military-ig-finds/
    text: Key Points and Summary – A Pentagon Inspector General review found the Army
      and Navy miscalculated Category IV enlistments—AFQT scores in the 10th–30th percentile—by
      using improved prep-course scores instead of initial results. -That approach let
      both services exceed the 4% statutory cap without required Secretary approval
      and congressional notification. -The Navy also ran a pilot […] The post U.S. Army
      and U.S. Navy Miscalculated Number of Low-Scoring Recruits Entering U.S. Military,
      IG Finds appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: A Pentagon Inspector General review revealed that the Army
      and Navy miscalculated the number of low-scoring recruits by using improved prep-course
      scores instead of initial AFQT results, allowing them to exceed the 4% statutory
      cap without necessary approvals.
    paragraph_summary: A Pentagon Inspector General review revealed that the Army and
      Navy miscalculated their enlistments of Category IV recruits—those with Armed
      Forces Qualification Test (AFQT) scores in the 10th to 30th percentile—by relying
      on improved scores from prep courses rather than initial test results. This miscalculation
      allowed both branches to exceed the 4% statutory cap on low-scoring recruits without
      obtaining the necessary approval from the Secretary of Defense or notifying Congress.
      Additionally, the Navy conducted a pilot program related to this issue.
    published: '2025-12-17T23:52:07+00:00'

  - title: The U.S. Military’s On Again, Off Again War on Shaving
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/the-u-s-militarys-on-again-off-again-war-on-shaving/
    text: Key Points and Summary – Military beards were common in the Civil War, but
      World War I gas-mask requirements made clean-shaven faces the norm. -The Navy
      briefly reversed course in 1970 under Adm. Elmo Zumwalt, then reinstated the ban
      in 1984. -After 9/11, some special operators grew beards overseas, while religious
      and medical waivers expanded […] The post The U.S. Military’s On Again, Off Again
      War on Shaving appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: The U.S. military's stance on beards has fluctuated over time,
      from their prevalence during the Civil War to a clean-shaven requirement during
      World War I, a brief allowance in the Navy in the 1970s, and a resurgence of beards
      among special operators post-9/11, reflecting ongoing debates about grooming standards.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the fluctuating policies regarding facial
      hair in the U.S. military, highlighting that while beards were common during the
      Civil War, World War I's gas-mask requirements led to a clean-shaven standard.
      In 1970, under Adm. Elmo Zumwalt, the Navy briefly allowed beards, but this was
      reversed in 1984. Following the events of 9/11, some special operators began growing
      beards in overseas deployments, and the military has since expanded religious
      and medical waivers regarding shaving, reflecting an ongoing debate about grooming
      standards.
    published: '2025-12-17T23:26:10+00:00'

  - title: The Air Force’s Mach 3 XB-70 Has a Message for the Stealth B-21 Raider Bomber
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/the-air-forces-mach-3-xb-70-has-a-message-for-the-stealth-b-21-raider-bomber/
    text: 'Key Points and Summary – The B-21 Raider is billed as the backbone of U.S.
      long-range strike, but history offers a warning. -The Mach-3 XB-70 Valkyrie met
      its engineering goals yet died when Soviet air defenses and ICBMs erased its mission.
      -The B-21 faces a different contest: improving sensors, space-based radar concepts,
      drones, and layered […] The post The Air Force’s Mach 3 XB-70 Has a Message for
      the Stealth B-21 Raider Bomber appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The B-21 Raider, intended as the cornerstone of U.S. long-range
      strike capabilities, faces challenges similar to those of the XB-70 Valkyrie,
      which, despite meeting its engineering goals, became obsolete due to advancements
      in enemy defenses and technology.
    paragraph_summary: The B-21 Raider is positioned as a crucial component of the U.S.
      long-range strike capabilities, but historical precedents, such as the Mach-3
      XB-70 Valkyrie, serve as cautionary tales. Despite the XB-70 achieving its engineering
      objectives, it was rendered obsolete by advancements in Soviet air defenses and
      intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs). The B-21 faces a different set of
      challenges, including the evolution of sensors, space-based radar technologies,
      drones, and multi-layered defense systems, which could impact its effectiveness
      in modern warfare.
    published: '2025-12-17T20:57:46+00:00'

    text: 'Key Points and Summary – The Air Force plans to keep 76 B-52s flying into

      delays are pushing schedules right and driving costs up. -A Nunn-McCurdy breach
      raises the stakes: if modernization slips further, long-range strike capacity
      could tighten fast. -The B-52 is […] The post A B-52J Bomber Crisis Means a B-21
      Raider Bomber Crisis appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The Air Force's B-52J upgrade, essential for maintaining long-range
      strike capacity into the 2050s, faces delays and rising costs due to issues with
      engine, radar, and weapons integration, raising concerns about modernization and
      its implications for the B-21 Raider bomber program.
    paragraph_summary: The U.S. Air Force intends to maintain 76 B-52 bombers operational
      into the 2050s with the B-52J upgrade; however, delays in engine, radar, and weapons
      integration are causing schedule setbacks and increasing costs. A Nunn-McCurdy
      breach heightens concerns, as further delays in modernization could significantly
      impact long-range strike capabilities. This situation raises alarms not only for
      the B-52 program but also for the B-21 Raider bomber, indicating a broader crisis
      in the Air Force's long-range strike strategy.

      all jets returned safely and later admitted a separate F-35 had been damaged by
      a bird strike, a coincidence Moscow spun into “proof” that obsolete Soviet SAMs
      […] The post Did a Russian-Made Missile Hit an F-35I Adir Stealth Fighter? appeared
      first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: In 2017, Russian and pro-Assad sources falsely claimed that
      a Syrian S-200 missile had struck an Israeli F-35I Adir, while the IDF confirmed
      all jets returned safely and attributed damage to a bird strike, which Moscow
      misrepresented as evidence against the F-35's capabilities.
    paragraph_summary: In 2017, Russian and pro-Assad media reported that a Syrian S-200
      missile had successfully struck an Israeli F-35I Adir fighter jet over Syria.
      However, the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) confirmed that all their jets returned
      safely and later clarified that a different F-35 had sustained damage due to a
      bird strike, which Moscow misinterpreted as evidence that outdated Soviet surface-to-air
      missiles could effectively target modern stealth aircraft.

    text: 'Key Points and Summary – The U.S. Navy once touted the electromagnetic railgun

    one_sentence_summary: The U.S. Navy abandoned its ambitious electromagnetic railgun
      project, which promised high-speed, long-range capabilities, after 15 years and
      over $500 million due to engineering challenges, including rapid barrel wear.
    paragraph_summary: The U.S. Navy's ambitious electromagnetic railgun project, which
      promised high-speed Mach 7 projectiles with a 100-nautical-mile range and cost-effective,
      gunpowder-free ammunition, was ultimately abandoned in 2021 after 15 years and
      over $500 million in investment. The program faced insurmountable engineering
      challenges, including barrel degradation after only a few dozen shots, leading
      to its discontinuation despite initial enthusiasm for its potential as a revolutionary
      naval weapon.

      Russia, highlighting a fundamental limitation that cannot be rectified.

    paragraph_summary: For ten years, the MiG-25 Foxbat was perceived as a formidable
      threat to Western air superiority, regarded as a titanium Mach-3 super-fighter
      that surpassed all competitors. However, the 1976 defection of Russian pilot Viktor
      Belenko to Japan allowed U.S. engineers to examine the aircraft closely, debunking
      its mythic status. They discovered that the MiG-25 was primarily constructed from
      steel and was a highly specialized interceptor, revealing its limitations and
      high fuel consumption, which contrasted sharply with its fearsome reputation.

  - title: The Mach 15 X-43D ‘Hypersonic Scramjet’ Has a Message for the Air Force
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/the-mach-15-x-43d-hypersonic-scramjet-has-a-message-for-the-air-force/
    text: Key Points and Summary – NASA’s Hyper-X program proved hydrogen-fueled scramjet
      flight with the X-43A at Mach 7–10, but its planned follow-on, the Mach 15 X-43D,
      died on the drawing board as budgets, leadership priorities, and agency restructurings
      shifted. -That vehicle was meant to gather real flight data in extreme hypersonic
      conditions and cut risk […] The post The Mach 15 X-43D ‘Hypersonic Scramjet’ Has
      a Message for the Air Force appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: NASA's Hyper-X program successfully demonstrated hydrogen-fueled
      scramjet flight with the X-43A at speeds of Mach 7-10, but the planned Mach 15
      X-43D was ultimately canceled due to shifting budgets and priorities, highlighting
      the need for real flight data in hypersonic conditions for the Air Force.
    paragraph_summary: NASA's Hyper-X program successfully demonstrated hydrogen-fueled
      scramjet flight with the X-43A, achieving speeds of Mach 7 to 10. However, the
      subsequent planned vehicle, the Mach 15 X-43D, was ultimately canceled due to
      shifting budgets, leadership priorities, and organizational changes within the
      agency. The X-43D was intended to collect real flight data under extreme hypersonic
      conditions to mitigate risks for future hypersonic technologies, highlighting
      a missed opportunity for the Air Force in advancing its capabilities in this area.
    published: '2025-12-13T13:15:43+00:00'

    text: Key Points and Summary – The Su-57 Felon was meant to anchor Russia’s fifth-generation
      air power and compete with America’s F-22 and F-35 and China’s J-20. -Instead,
      it has become a symbol of Russia’s industrial limits. Fewer than 20 serial jets

    one_sentence_summary: The Su-57 Felon, intended to establish Russia's fifth-generation
      air superiority against the F-22, F-35, and J-20, has instead highlighted the
      country's industrial shortcomings, with production lagging and fewer than 20 operational
      jets.
    paragraph_summary: The Su-57 Felon, intended to serve as the cornerstone of Russia's
      fifth-generation air power and rival the U.S. F-22 and F-35 as well as China's
      J-20, has instead highlighted the country's industrial shortcomings. With fewer
      than 20 serial jets produced and an annual output of only two to four units, the
      fighter's development has been sluggish, and it has yet to receive its long-promised
      Izdeliye-30 engines. This situation raises questions about the aircraft's effectiveness
      as a stealth fighter.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/saab-37-viggen-has-a-message-for-the-u-s-air-force-f-35-stealth-fighter/
    text: 'Key Points and Article Summary: Sweden’s Saab 37 Viggen was purpose-built
      for a particular Cold War concept: disperse fighters onto highway strips under
      the Bas 60 and later Bas 90 basing systems so the Soviet Union could never wipe
      out the Swedish Air Force in a first strike. -Its single afterburning engine,
      thrust reverser, and […] The post Saab 37 Viggen Has a Message for the U.S. Air
      Force F-35 Stealth Fighter appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The Saab 37 Viggen was designed during the Cold War to ensure
      the Swedish Air Force's survivability against a Soviet first strike by utilizing
      highway strips for deployment, offering lessons for the U.S. Air Force's F-35
      stealth fighter.
    paragraph_summary: The Saab 37 Viggen was designed during the Cold War to enhance
      Sweden's air defense by enabling the deployment of fighters on highway strips,
      thereby preventing the Soviet Union from easily targeting the Swedish Air Force
      in a surprise attack. Its unique features, such as a single afterburning engine
      and thrust reverser, highlight its adaptability and operational strategy. The
      article suggests that the Viggen's design principles could offer valuable insights
      for the U.S. Air Force's F-35 stealth fighter, particularly in terms of survivability
      and operational flexibility in modern warfare.
    published: '2025-12-12T15:21:02+00:00'

      submarine-launched ballistic missiles (SLBMs) rendered the Valkyrie's design increasingly
      obsolete, highlighting the need for the Air Force to adapt to evolving threats
      in aerial warfare.

      as it aims to both develop a fleet of carriers and deploy advanced anti-access/area

      to deter U.S. intervention in regional conflicts, particularly over Taiwan and

      of aircraft carriers is still deemed essential for power projection.

  - title: The F-19 Stealth Fighter Has a Message for the U.S. Air Force
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/the-f-19-stealth-fighter-has-a-message-for-the-u-s-air-force/
    text: Key Points and Summary – For much of the 1980s, the “F-19” was the most famous
      fighter jet never built. -A skipped designation between the F/A-18 and F-20, Cold
      War secrecy, and whispers about radar-evading “black projects” convinced the public—and
      some foreign militaries—that a secret F-19 stealth fighter existed. -Model-maker
      Revell turned the myth into […] The post The F-19 Stealth Fighter Has a Message
      for the U.S. Air Force appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: The F-19 stealth fighter, a legendary yet unbuilt aircraft
      from the 1980s, symbolizes the impact of Cold War secrecy and public fascination
      with advanced military technology, serving as a cautionary tale for the U.S. Air
      Force.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the F-19, a legendary fighter jet that
      never actually existed, which became a symbol of Cold War intrigue during the
      1980s. Its skipped designation between the F/A-18 and F-20, along with rumors
      of radar-evading "black projects," fueled public and military speculation about
      its existence. Model-maker Revell capitalized on this myth, further embedding
      the F-19 in popular culture. The piece suggests that the story of the F-19 carries
      a relevant message for the U.S. Air Force today, likely highlighting the importance
      of transparency and communication in military advancements.
    published: '2025-12-08T23:36:22+00:00'

  - title: Germany’s ‘Pocket’ Battleships Have a Message for Every Navy on Earth
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/germanys-pocket-battleships-have-a-message-for-every-navy-on-earth/
    text: Key Points and Summary – Germany’s so-called “pocket battleships” — Deutschland,
      Admiral Scheer, and Admiral Graf Spee — were Hitler’s workaround to interwar naval
      limits, combining diesel propulsion, 11-inch guns, and long range in relatively
      light hulls. -Optimized to terrorize merchant shipping, they found early success
      in commerce raiding but proved too lightly armored and […] The post Germany’s
      ‘Pocket’ Battleships Have a Message for Every Navy on Earth appeared first on
      19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: Germany's "pocket battleships," including the Deutschland,
      Admiral Scheer, and Admiral Graf Spee, were designed to circumvent interwar naval
      restrictions with their unique combination of diesel engines, 11-inch guns, and
      long range, effectively targeting merchant shipping despite their vulnerabilities
      in armor.
    paragraph_summary: Germany's "pocket battleships"—the Deutschland, Admiral Scheer,
      and Admiral Graf Spee—were designed by Hitler as a means to circumvent the naval
      restrictions imposed after World War I. These ships featured diesel propulsion,
      11-inch guns, and long-range capabilities within a relatively lightweight framework,
      making them effective for commerce raiding against merchant shipping. However,
      their success was limited by their inadequate armor, highlighting important lessons
      for modern navies regarding the balance between firepower, armor, and operational
      strategy.
    published: '2025-12-08T20:37:32+00:00'

    text: Key Points and Summary – The F-16XL was General Dynamics’ bold attempt to

      effort to transform the lightweight F-16 into a long-range strike fighter, featuring
      a significantly larger cranked-arrow delta wing that allowed it to carry approximately
      three times the hardpoints and more fuel than its predecessor. This design improved

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/j-10-vs-f-16-the-secret-israeli-dna-in-chinas-vigorous-dragon-fighter/
    text: 'Key Points and Summary – China’s J-10 “Vigorous Dragon” was billed as Beijing’s
      homegrown answer to the F-16, but its real origins are far more complicated. -In
      the 1990s, as Israel sought export markets for its canceled Lavi fighter, key
      technologies in avionics, flight controls, composites, missiles, and sensors quietly
      flowed to China’s Chengdu Aircraft […] The post J-10 vs. F-16: The Secret Israeli
      DNA in China’s ‘Vigorous Dragon’ Fighter appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: China's J-10 fighter, marketed as a domestic alternative to
      the F-16, actually incorporates significant Israeli technology from the 1990s,
      stemming from the canceled Lavi fighter program.
    paragraph_summary: China's J-10 fighter, known as the "Vigorous Dragon," was initially
      presented as a domestic alternative to the F-16, but its development is rooted
      in a complex history involving foreign technology transfers. In the 1990s, Israel,
      looking to market its canceled Lavi fighter, inadvertently provided China’s Chengdu
      Aircraft with crucial technologies related to avionics, flight controls, composites,
      missiles, and sensors. This collaboration highlights the intricate and often secretive
      connections between nations in the aerospace sector, revealing the J-10's reliance
      on Israeli innovations despite its portrayal as a purely Chinese creation.

      successfully infiltrating the defenses of the USS Ronald Reagan, highlighting

      warfare.

    paragraph_summary: The USS Missouri (BB-63), famously known for hosting Japan's

      bombarding Iwo Jima and Okinawa, engaging in aerial combat, and enduring kamikaze
      attacks while also supporting operations against Japan's Home Islands. The Missouri
      continued to serve in the Korean War, further solidifying its legacy as a formidable
      naval asset.

      where the demand for bomber presence from combatant commanders exceeds the capabilities
      of the current fleet. This issue is exacerbated by the aging of legacy bombers
      like the B-1B, B-2, and B-52, while the introduction of the new B-21 Raider is
      progressing slowly. As a result, there is a growing concern about a potential
      shortfall in bomber availability, which could pose risks to national security
      and military operations.

      on acquiring new technology.

      for modern stealth fighters like the F-35, particularly in terms of adaptability
      and survivability in diverse combat environments.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/donald-trump-revives-the-monroe-doctrine-and-gets-it-dangerously-wrong/
    text: Key Points and Summary – Donald Trump’s anniversary proclamation for the Monroe
      Doctrine adds a “Trump Corollary,” vowing that only Americans will shape their
      hemisphere’s destiny. -Dr. Michael Rubin argues this “Donroe Doctrine” misunderstands
      Monroe’s intent and today’s reality. -Monroe paired Western-hemisphere vigilance
      with noninterference elsewhere. -Trump, by contrast, flirts with 21st-century
      isolationism just as […] The post Donald Trump Revives the Monroe Doctrine – and
      Gets It Dangerously Wrong appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: Donald Trump's anniversary proclamation for the Monroe Doctrine
      introduces a "Trump Corollary" that asserts American dominance in shaping the
      hemisphere's future, but Dr. Michael Rubin argues this misinterprets Monroe's
      original intent of vigilance coupled with noninterference and risks promoting
      modern isolationism.
    paragraph_summary: In a recent proclamation commemorating the Monroe Doctrine, Donald
      Trump introduced a "Trump Corollary," asserting that only Americans should determine
      the future of the Western Hemisphere. Dr. Michael Rubin critiques this interpretation,
      suggesting that it misrepresents the original intent of the Monroe Doctrine, which
      balanced vigilance in the Western Hemisphere with a policy of noninterference
      in other regions. Rubin warns that Trump's approach leans towards a form of 21st-century
      isolationism, diverging from the historical principles established by Monroe.
    published: '2025-12-05T12:50:01+00:00'

    text: 'Key Points and Summary – Months before Chernobyl, the Soviet Navy suffered
      a major nuclear disaster when the Echo-II submarine K-431 blew its reactor during
      “routine” refueling in Chazhma Bay near Vladivostok. -A mishandled reactor lid
      triggered a prompt criticality, killing nearly a dozen sailors and irradiating
      hundreds more as radioactive debris showered nearby ships […] The post Mini Chernobyl:
      The Secret Russian Navy Nuclear Submarine Meltdown Moscow Tried to Bury appeared
      first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: Months before the Chernobyl disaster, the Soviet Navy's Echo-II
      submarine K-431 experienced a catastrophic reactor meltdown during routine refueling
      in Chazhma Bay, resulting in the deaths of nearly a dozen sailors and widespread
      radiation exposure to hundreds more.
    paragraph_summary: Months prior to the Chernobyl disaster, the Soviet Navy experienced
      a significant nuclear incident when the Echo-II submarine K-431's reactor exploded
      during routine refueling in Chazhma Bay, near Vladivostok. A mishandled reactor
      lid led to a prompt criticality, resulting in the deaths of nearly a dozen sailors
      and exposing hundreds more to radiation as radioactive debris fell onto nearby
      vessels. This event, often referred to as a "mini Chernobyl," was largely concealed
      by the Soviet authorities.

      targets up to 2,000 miles away. This necessitates a fighter with nearly double
      the range of the F-35C, as well as capabilities for real on-station dwell time
      and deep-strike missions. The article emphasizes that to effectively operate in
      this challenging environment, the F/A-XX must function as a long-range "sniper"
      to ensure the safety and effectiveness of naval operations.
    published: '2025-12-04T17:41:00+00:00'

      agreements.

      nuclear power in the context of military capabilities, particularly regarding
      the potential replacement of its diesel submarines with nuclear-powered ones.
      This shift in perspective has been influenced by recent developments, including
      a U.S.–South Korea nuclear submarine agreement, China's expanding naval presence,
      and increased tensions surrounding Taiwan. As Japan evaluates its postwar nuclear
      policies, the debate over adopting nuclear submarines marks a significant change
      in its defense strategy, reflecting the evolving security landscape in the region.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/canada-has-a-message-for-the-f-a-18-super-hornet-fighter/
    text: Key Points and Summary – Canada’s plan to replace its aging CF-18 fleet turned
      into a political and industrial drama that ultimately doomed Boeing’s F/A-18 Super
      Hornet. -Ottawa dropped the Super Hornet from its 88-jet competition after Boeing
      launched a trade case against Canadian aerospace champion Bombardier, prompting
      new rules penalizing firms seen as harming […] The post Canada Has a Message for
      the F/A-18 Super Hornet Fighter appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: Canada's decision to exclude Boeing's F/A-18 Super Hornet
      from its fighter jet competition stemmed from a political fallout following Boeing's
      trade dispute with Bombardier, leading to new rules that penalized companies perceived
      as detrimental to Canadian industry.
    paragraph_summary: Canada's decision to replace its aging CF-18 fleet has led to
      significant political and industrial tensions, ultimately resulting in the exclusion
      of Boeing's F/A-18 Super Hornet from the competition for 88 new jets. This decision
      followed Boeing's trade case against Canadian aerospace company Bombardier, which
      prompted Canada to implement new rules that penalize companies perceived as undermining
      local industries. The situation highlights the complexities and repercussions
      of international trade disputes on defense procurement processes.

    text: 'Key Points and Summary – After losing the Air Force’s Next Generation Air
      Dominance contest to Boeing’s F-47, Lockheed Martin is pushing an aggressive Plan
      B: a “Ferrari” F-35. -CEO Jim Taiclet says the company can deliver roughly 80
      percent of sixth-generation capability at half the cost by grafting NGAD-era tech
      onto the F-35 airframe. […] The post Forget the F-47 NGAD: Is a Supercharged ‘Ferrari’
      F-35 the Real Next U.S. Air Force Fighter? appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: After losing the Next Generation Air Dominance contest to
      Boeing's F-47, Lockheed Martin plans to enhance the F-35 with advanced technology
      to achieve significant sixth-generation capabilities at a lower cost, positioning
      it as a potential alternative for the U.S. Air Force.
    paragraph_summary: After losing the Air Force's Next Generation Air Dominance (NGAD)
      competition to Boeing's F-47, Lockheed Martin is pivoting to an ambitious alternative
      strategy, proposing a high-performance version of the F-35, dubbed the "Ferrari"
      F-35. CEO Jim Taiclet claims that this upgraded model can achieve approximately
      80% of sixth-generation capabilities at half the cost by integrating advanced
      NGAD technologies into the existing F-35 airframe. This approach positions the
      F-35 as a potential frontrunner for the future of U.S. Air Force fighter aircraft.

    one_sentence_summary: The U.S. has capped F-22 Raptor production at 187 jets due
      to budget reallocations, despite its status as the world's top air-superiority
      fighter, leaving military leaders concerned about the decision.
    paragraph_summary: The F-22 Raptor, considered the world's leading air-superiority
      fighter, will not see any further production beyond the 187 jets already built,
      a decision made by former Defense Secretary Bob Gates in 2009 to allocate resources
      towards the B-21 bomber and counterinsurgency efforts. This decision has led to
      frustration among military leaders, who view it as a significant oversight given
      the aircraft's unmatched capabilities in air combat.

    text: Key Points and Summary – The MiG-35 was sold as Russia’s affordable, export-ready
      answer to the F-16 and Gripen—a “4++” bridge between aging MiG-29s and modern
      air combat. -In reality, it never delivered. -The promised AESA radar and advanced
      engines failed to materialize in operational jets, leaving a warmed-over MiG-29
      in a fifth-generation world. -Moscow […] The post Russia’s MiG-35 Fighter Fiasco
      appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: The MiG-35, marketed as Russia's cost-effective alternative
      to the F-16 and Gripen, ultimately fell short of expectations due to the absence
      of promised advanced technology, resulting in a fighter that resembles an outdated
      MiG-29 in a modern combat landscape.
    paragraph_summary: The MiG-35 was marketed by Russia as an affordable, export-ready
      alternative to the F-16 and Gripen, positioned as a "4++" fighter to bridge the
      gap between outdated MiG-29s and modern air combat capabilities. However, it has
      not lived up to expectations, as the anticipated advanced features like AESA radar
      and modern engines were not included in the operational jets, resulting in a fighter
      that essentially resembles an upgraded MiG-29 rather than a competitive option
      in the fifth-generation landscape.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/12/russias-su-57-felon-stealth-fighter-might-not-even-be-a-stealth-fighter/
    text: Key Points and Summary – Russia’s Su-57 Felon was billed as a true fifth-generation
      rival to the F-22, F-35, and China’s J-20. -Instead, it has become a low-volume,
      high-hype program. -Chronic production bottlenecks, sanctions, engine delays,
      and questionable stealth features mean fewer than 20 serial jets likely exist,
      all flying with a stopgap fourth-generation powerplant. […] The post Russia’s
      Su-57 Felon Stealth Fighter Might Not Even Be a Stealth Fighter appeared first
      on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: Russia's Su-57 Felon, initially promoted as a fifth-generation
      stealth fighter to rival the F-22, F-35, and China's J-20, has faced significant
      production challenges and limitations, resulting in fewer than 20 operational
      jets that rely on outdated technology.
    paragraph_summary: Russia's Su-57 Felon was initially promoted as a formidable fifth-generation
      stealth fighter to compete with the F-22, F-35, and China's J-20. However, it
      has turned into a low-volume, high-hype program plagued by production bottlenecks,
      sanctions, engine delays, and doubts about its stealth capabilities. As a result,
      it is estimated that fewer than 20 operational jets exist, all currently utilizing
      a temporary fourth-generation engine instead of the intended advanced powerplant.

    one_sentence_summary: The F-22 Raptor, initially intended as America's leading air

      a 2009 decision to cap production at 187 jets. This decision has resulted in program

      $300 million. Consequently, the operational cost of flying each Raptor now exceeds
      $334,000, making it the most expensive fighter jet in history.

      and the future of air-breathing flight technology.

      in the context of evolving warfare in the Indo-Pacific region, where drones and
      multirole jets are increasingly taking on CAS responsibilities. However, supporters
      of the A-10 argue that it cannot be directly replaced, highlighting its unique
      capabilities and effectiveness in ground support missions.

      aircraft carrier fleet, which played a crucial role in NATO's anti-submarine warfare

      vital shipping lanes. However, despite their importance, Canada no longer operates
      aircraft carriers, raising questions about the reasons behind their disappearance
      from the Royal Canadian Navy's capabilities.

    paragraph_summary: The Casablanca-class escort carrier (CVE) played a crucial yet
      often overlooked role in World War II, as it was mass-produced by industrialist
      Henry Kaiser to counter the Japanese Navy. Utilizing innovative assembly-line
      techniques, Kaiser was able to produce 50 of these "Jeep Carriers" in just two
      years, averaging one every three weeks. Despite their small size of 10,000 tons
      and being criticized as "combustible," these carriers significantly contributed
      to naval operations during the war, showcasing a remarkable production achievement
      in shipbuilding.

    paragraph_summary: The USS Thresher (SSN-593) disaster in 1963, which resulted in
      the loss of the submarine and all 129 crew members, is the deadliest submarine
      incident in history and led to the establishment of crucial safety protocols for
      U.S. Navy submarines. The tragedy was attributed to a failure in a saltwater piping
      system that flooded the engine room, leading to a reactor shutdown and the loss
      of propulsion during deep-dive trials. This incident highlighted the need for
      improved safety measures, ultimately shaping the protocols that protect sailors
      today.

    paragraph_summary: The XB-70 Valkyrie was a groundbreaking U.S. Air Force bomber
      developed in the 1950s, designed to fly at Mach 3 and reach altitudes of 70,000
      feet, aiming to evade Soviet air defenses and replace the B-52 and B-58 bombers.
      Although it took its first flight in 1964, advancements in Soviet surface-to-air
      missile technology and intercontinental ballistic missiles had already begun to
      alter the strategic landscape, raising questions about the relevance of the XB-70's
      design. The article suggests that the lessons learned from the XB-70's development
      and operational challenges could offer valuable insights for the Air Force in
      addressing modern aerial threats.

      for stealth, supercruise capabilities, impressive maneuverability, and advanced
      sensors, but it ultimately fell short in terms of production scale. Originally

      War complacency, rising unit costs, and changing military priorities, resulting
      in a limited fleet that poses ongoing challenges for the Air Force.

  - title: '‘We Left A Manhole Open’: How A New Navy Nuclear Submarine Sank While Docked'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/11/we-left-a-manhole-open-how-a-new-navy-nuclear-submarine-sank-while-docked/
    text: 'Key Points and Summary – In 1969, the brand-new nuclear attack submarine
      USS Guitarro famously “sank” pierside at Mare Island after a stunning series of
      blunders. -Workers removed a bolted manhole cover and cofferdam in the bow sonar
      dome to swap out faulty transducers—and never put them back. -Weeks later, simultaneous
      trimming and calibration tests […] The post ‘We Left A Manhole Open’: How A New
      Navy Nuclear Submarine Sank While Docked appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: In 1969, the USS Guitarro, a newly commissioned nuclear submarine,
      sank at Mare Island due to a series of mistakes, including the failure to replace
      a manhole cover and cofferdam after maintenance work.
    paragraph_summary: In 1969, the USS Guitarro, a newly commissioned nuclear attack
      submarine, infamously sank while docked at Mare Island due to a series of critical
      mistakes. Workers had removed a bolted manhole cover and cofferdam from the bow
      sonar dome to replace faulty transducers but failed to reinstall them. This oversight,
      combined with simultaneous trimming and calibration tests, led to the submarine
      taking on water and ultimately sinking at the pier.
    published: '2025-11-30T12:25:52+00:00'

    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the Admiral Kuznetsov, a Russian aircraft
      carrier originally designed as a "heavy aircraft-carrying cruiser" to circumvent
      the Montreux Convention. Despite its problematic mazut engines, which produced
      thick black smoke and frequent breakdowns, the ship remained operational for decades
      following the Soviet Union's collapse, often becoming a target of ridicule among
      NATO forces. The piece highlights ongoing concerns within the Navy regarding the
      vessel's seaworthiness, with fears that it might sink due to its long history

      to maintaining and enhancing its strategic bomber capabilities.

      Air Dominance (NGAD) program uncertain regarding the number of airframes and their
      timeline, and in light of advanced fighter developments by Russia and China, the
      Air Force plans to upgrade its existing F-22s for service well into the 2050s.

      “Vought 1600.” -Engineers stretched and strengthened the F-16, added a tailhook,
      and […] The post The F-16 Fighter Has A Clear Message for the U.S. Navy and Its
      Aircraft Carriers appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: In the 1970s, the Air Force's F-16 fighter was nearly adapted
      for naval use as the "Vought 1600" under Pentagon pressure to reduce costs and
      streamline military fleets, highlighting ongoing discussions about the Navy's
      aircraft carrier capabilities.
    paragraph_summary: In the 1970s, the U.S. Air Force's F-16 fighter jet was considered
      for adaptation to naval use as the "Vought 1600" amid Pentagon efforts to reduce
      costs and streamline military fleets. Engineers modified the F-16 by stretching
      and reinforcing its structure and adding a tailhook for carrier operations. This
      historical context highlights the ongoing relevance of the F-16's design and capabilities,
      suggesting that lessons learned from its development could inform the U.S. Navy's
      approach to aircraft carriers and future naval aviation strategies.

      to the submarine but only minor harm to the aircraft carrier, which U.S. officers
      attributed to poor Soviet seamanship.
    paragraph_summary: In 1984, the Soviet Victor-class submarine K-314 collided with
      the USS Kitty Hawk during nighttime exercises in the Sea of Japan, resulting in
      significant damage to the submarine while the aircraft carrier sustained only
      minor injuries. U.S. officials attributed the incident to poor seamanship on the
      part of the Soviet crew, highlighting the potential for disaster given the submarine's
      nuclear capabilities. The event underscored the tense military dynamics of the
      Cold War era.

    text: Key Points and Summary – The US Navy has taken a pragmatic approach to titanium,

      signature made it attractive for Soviet designers, who built titanium-hulled boats
      like the Papa and Sierra classes and […] The post Why the Navy Never Built ‘Deep
      Diving’ Titanium Submarines Like Russia appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: The US Navy opts for a practical use of titanium in high-stress

      with Soviet designs that utilized titanium hulls for their submarines.
    paragraph_summary: The US Navy has opted for a practical use of titanium, employing
      it selectively in high-stress components rather than constructing entire hulls
      from the metal, unlike the Soviet Union, which utilized titanium extensively for
      submarines such as the Papa and Sierra classes due to its strength, corrosion
      resistance, and low magnetic signature. This strategic choice reflects the Navy's
      focus on efficiency and effectiveness in submarine design, steering away from
      the deep-diving titanium submarines that Russia pursued.

      combat scenario between the two fighters.

    paragraph_summary: The B-1B Lancer was originally designed as a versatile Cold War
      bomber to replace the B-58 and B-52, combining speed, range, and payload capabilities.

      aircraft in a modern military landscape dominated by advanced systems like the
      S-400. Isaac Seitz discusses the design compromises made during its development,
      including reduced speed and the loss of nuclear and cruise missile capabilities,
      highlighting that these fundamental issues cannot be rectified, raising concerns
      about the Lancer's future viability.

    one_sentence_summary: The retirement of four Ohio-class SSGNs and Ticonderoga-class
      cruisers by 2027 poses a significant challenge for the U.S. Navy, as these vessels
      currently serve as crucial platforms for launching Tomahawk missiles.
    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the transformation of four Ohio-class submarines
      into SSGNs (guided missile submarines) after post-Cold War cuts, allowing each
      to carry 154 Tomahawk cruise missiles in repurposed Trident tubes. Together with
      Ticonderoga-class cruisers, these vessels create a formidable arsenal with 2,080
      vertical-launch cells, effectively serving as America's floating missile magazines.
      However, concerns are rising as all four SSGNs and every Ticonderoga-class cruiser
      are scheduled for retirement by 2027, which could significantly impact the U.S.
      Navy's missile capabilities.

      technical disagreements, and escalating costs, leading Germany to withdraw from
      the project in 1969. The article reflects on how the challenges faced by the MBT-70
      were unforeseen, resulting in a significant setback for military tank development.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/11/the-b-21-raider-might-have-a-battleship-problem/
    text: Article Summary – Talk of drones and AI “revolutionizing” warfare repeats
      the same RMA hype of the 1990s. Technologies like the B-21 Raider, unmanned systems,
      and AI are powerful, but they are evolutionary advances, not game-changers that
      alter war’s fundamental character. -The B-21 still performs classic missions—deterrence,
      deep strike, nuclear and conventional signaling—only with better […] The post
      The B-21 Raider Might Have a ‘Battleship’ Problem appeared first on 19FortyFive
      .
    one_sentence_summary: The article argues that while technologies like the B-21 Raider
      and AI are significant advancements in warfare, they represent evolutionary rather
      than revolutionary changes, continuing to fulfill traditional military roles rather
      than fundamentally altering the nature of war.
    paragraph_summary: The article argues that the current excitement surrounding drones
      and AI in warfare mirrors the hype of the 1990s regarding Revolutionary Military
      Affairs (RMA). While technologies like the B-21 Raider and unmanned systems represent
      significant advancements, they do not fundamentally change the nature of warfare;
      rather, they enhance traditional military missions such as deterrence and deep
      strikes. The B-21, despite its advanced capabilities, still fulfills classic roles,
      suggesting that these innovations are evolutionary rather than revolutionary,
      akin to the historical challenges faced by battleships in adapting to new forms
      of warfare.
    published: '2025-11-25T12:17:51+00:00'

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/11/why-the-navy-crunched-the-flying-dorito-a-12-avenger-ii-stealth-bomber/
    text: Article Summary – The A-12 Avenger II was the Navy’s bid to put a stealth
      strike jet on carrier decks after the F-117’s debut, a flying-wing “Flying Dorito”
      built to sneak in first and kill enemy radars. -Instead, cost overruns, weight
      growth, secrecy, and mismanagement led to its 1991 cancellation after $5 billion
      spent. -The […] The post Why The Navy Crunched the ‘Flying Dorito’ A-12 Avenger
      II Stealth Bomber appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: The A-12 Avenger II, a stealth strike jet designed for the
      Navy, was canceled in 1991 after $5 billion was spent due to cost overruns, weight
      issues, secrecy, and mismanagement.
    paragraph_summary: The A-12 Avenger II was the Navy's attempt to develop a stealth
      strike jet for aircraft carriers, inspired by the success of the F-117. Designed
      as a flying-wing aircraft, nicknamed the "Flying Dorito," it aimed to infiltrate
      enemy airspace undetected and disable radar systems. However, the project faced
      significant challenges, including cost overruns, weight increases, excessive secrecy,
      and mismanagement, ultimately leading to its cancellation in 1991 after $5 billion
      had been spent.

    paragraph_summary: The article discusses the transformation of the U.S. Navy's Iowa-class
      battleships during the Reagan era, as they were upgraded to meet the challenges
      posed by a rising Soviet threat. Originally designed as World War II gun platforms,
      these battleships were modernized into multi-role warships equipped with advanced
      weaponry, including Tomahawk land-attack missiles, Harpoon anti-ship missiles,
      and Phalanx Close-In Weapon Systems (CIWS) for defense. Additionally, they received
      modern radars, combat systems, and electronic warfare capabilities, effectively
      dragging them into the missile age and enhancing their operational versatility.

    one_sentence_summary: France's Charles de Gaulle (R91), commissioned in 2001, is

      equipped with advanced reactors for extended endurance.
    paragraph_summary: France's Charles de Gaulle (R91) is the nation's sole aircraft
      carrier and the first domestically constructed nuclear-powered vessel, commissioned
      in 2001. Weighing 42,000 tons, it employs CATOBAR (Catapult Assisted Take-Off
      But Arrested Recovery) operations to deploy Rafale M fighter jets, E-2C Hawkeye
      surveillance aircraft, and helicopters for various missions including strike,
      air defense, and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR). Powered
      by two K15 reactors, the carrier boasts impressive endurance and is equipped with
      advanced Aster 15 and Mistral missile systems, enhancing its operational capabilities.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/11/why-the-mach-2-f-105-thud-was-loved-by-pilots-despite-being-a-flying-coffin/
    text: Article Summary – The F-105 Thunderchief, or “Thud,” began life as a supersonic
      nuclear striker before becoming the U.S. Air Force’s primary fighter-bomber over
      North Vietnam. -Built by Republic Aviation, the big single-engine jet could haul
      a heavier bomb load than a WWII heavy bomber and still reach Mach 2. -In Vietnam,
      it flew the […] The post Why the Mach 2 F-105 ‘Thud’ Was Loved by Pilots—Despite
      Being a ‘Flying Coffin’ appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: The F-105 Thunderchief, originally designed as a supersonic
      nuclear striker, evolved into a primary fighter-bomber for the U.S. Air Force
      in Vietnam, known for its impressive bomb load capacity and speed, despite being
      regarded by some as a "flying coffin" due to its high risks in combat.
    paragraph_summary: The F-105 Thunderchief, affectionately known as the "Thud," was
      initially designed as a supersonic nuclear strike aircraft but evolved into the
      U.S. Air Force's main fighter-bomber during the Vietnam War. Manufactured by Republic
      Aviation, this powerful single-engine jet was capable of carrying a bomb load
      heavier than that of World War II heavy bombers while achieving speeds of Mach
      2. Despite its impressive capabilities, pilots often referred to the F-105 as
      a "flying coffin" due to its high casualty rates in combat, yet it remained a
      beloved aircraft among those who flew it.

    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/11/the-x-32-stealth-fighter-has-a-message-for-the-u-s-military/
    text: Key Points and Summary – The Joint Strike Fighter competition was supposed
      to deliver a single stealth jet for the Air Force, Navy, Marines and key allies.
      -It quickly became a duel between Boeing’s X-32 and Lockheed Martin’s X-35. The
      X-32 struggled with short-takeoff/vertical landing, required reconfiguration between
      modes, and drifted from its original design, […] The post The X-32 Stealth Fighter
      Has a Message for the U.S. Military appeared first on 19FortyFive .
    one_sentence_summary: The article discusses the challenges faced by Boeing's X-32
      in the Joint Strike Fighter competition against Lockheed Martin's X-35, highlighting
      its difficulties with short-takeoff/vertical landing and design deviations, which
      serve as a cautionary message for the U.S. military.
    paragraph_summary: The Joint Strike Fighter competition aimed to create a single
      stealth jet for the U.S. military and its allies, but it evolved into a contest
      between Boeing's X-32 and Lockheed Martin's X-35. The X-32 faced significant challenges,
      particularly with its short-takeoff/vertical landing capabilities, necessitating
      reconfiguration between flight modes and deviating from its initial design. The
      article suggests that the struggles of the X-32 serve as a cautionary tale for
      the U.S. military regarding the complexities and risks involved in developing
      advanced military aircraft.
    published: '2025-11-23T12:49:25+00:00'

      featuring a single engine, thin trapezoidal wings, and minimal avionics, prioritizing
      speed. This aircraft became notable for being the first fighter to sustain supersonic
      flight, and its development carries important lessons for the U.S. Air Force today.

      her versatility in escorting fast carriers, engaging shore targets, and asserting
      naval dominance. The article suggests that the USS Missouri carries a significant
      message for the current U.S. Navy, emphasizing the enduring legacy and lessons

  - title: 'No Place to Hide: The End of Submarine Stealth?'
    url: https://www.19fortyfive.com/2025/11/no-place-to-hide-the-end-of-submarine-stealth/
    text: 'Key Points and Summary – U.S. submarines still own the acoustic fight, but
      a wave of non-acoustic sensors is narrowing the gap. -A Naval Submarine League
      analysis spotlights magnetic anomaly detection (MAD), bioluminescent “boundary
      layer” wakes, surface and internal wave signatures, thermal trails seen by IR,
      and blue-green laser lidar that can ping through seawater. […] The post No Place
      to Hide: The End of Submarine Stealth? appeared first on 19FortyFive .'
    one_sentence_summary: The article discusses how while U.S. submarines maintain superiority
      in acoustic detection, emerging non-acoustic sensors like magnetic anomaly detection
      and thermal imaging are increasingly challenging their stealth capabilities.
    paragraph_summary: A recent analysis by the Naval Submarine League highlights that
      while U.S. submarines maintain superiority in acoustic detection, emerging non-acoustic
      sensors are increasingly challenging their stealth capabilities. Technologies
      such as magnetic anomaly detection (MAD), bioluminescent wakes, surface and internal
      wave signatures, infrared thermal trails, and blue-green laser lidar are becoming
      more effective at detecting submarines, potentially diminishing their ability
      to operate undetected. This shift raises concerns about the future of submarine
      stealth in naval warfare.
    published: '2025-11-10T20:47:29+00:00'

      Navy and recent provocations, Australia is reinforcing its undersea capabilities

      submarines, ensuring their operational status into the 2030s. While the AUKUS
      nuclear submarines are still years from deployment, the Collins-class submarines,
      which are quiet diesel-electric vessels equipped with advanced Mk 48 torpedoes,
      will play a crucial role in bolstering Australia's naval power during this transitional
      period.

      networking capabilities, leading to limited production and export opportunities.
    paragraph_summary: The MiG-35, Russia's latest version of the MiG-29, is a lightweight,
      agile multirole fighter equipped with advanced features such as AESA radar, enhanced
      electronic warfare capabilities, and precision-strike options. While it theoretically
      positions itself between late 4th generation and 5th generation fighter technology,
      it falls short in practical aspects like low observability, mature networking,
      and production scale. Consequently, production numbers remain limited, and export
      efforts to countries like Egypt and Vietnam have not yielded significant success.

      further complicating the carrier's potential return to service.
